query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures (500°C to 1200°C), HfNbTaTiZr undergoes a dislocation mechanism transition wherein thermal activation changes the core structure of dislocations from predominantly screw-character (at room temperature) to more mobile edge-character. This transition is accompanied by subtle changes in short-range chemical ordering, which together modulate the elastic moduli and thermal expansion behavior relative to the room temperature baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy with room temperature stress–strain, thermal expansion, and elastic properties measured in an unaltered state.
generation.intervention: In situ high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., uniaxial tensile/compressive tests and thermal expansion measurements) combined with atomistic or mesoscale simulations that track dislocation dynamics and short-range order evolution.
generation.conditions: The hypothesis is to be tested in a controlled environment within the temperature range of 500°C to 1200°C under varied strain rates and loadings, avoiding conditions that induce oxidation or phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced modifications in dislocation core structure (shift from screw-dominated to increased edge dislocation mobility) and evolving short-range chemical order among constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Raising the temperature provides sufficient thermal energy to facilitate a reconfiguration of dislocation cores, reducing the strength of the lattice pinning (typical of screw dislocations), thus enabling an increased role of edge dislocations in plastic flow. Concurrently, the thermal energy partially disrupts short-range chemical clustering, subtly altering the bond stiffness and lattice parameters. These combined effects lead to observable changes in yield stress, elastic moduli, and thermal expansion behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the room temperature baseline, elevated temperature tests will show (i) a distinct softening effect with a less pronounced yield point due to enhanced edge dislocation mobility, (ii) nonlinear thermal expansion behavior (such as a plateau or anomaly) that deviates from simple phonon-driven expansion, and (iii) a measurable shift in elastic moduli reflecting the altered dislocation and short-range order structure.
generation.baseline: Room temperature stress–strain curves, thermal expansion coefficients, and elastic moduli of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy in its as-synthesized BCC state.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to be valid strictly within the 500°C to 1200°C range. At temperatures below 500°C, traditional screw dislocation mechanisms dominate, while above 1200°C, additional effects such as oxidation or phase instability may come into play.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in dislocation character and the degree of short-range order disruption are not fully pre-determined, requiring detailed correlation between experimental observations and simulation data. Additionally, the interplay between dislocation dynamics and thermal expansion is complex and might vary with subtle changes in alloy processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile/compression and dilatometry) on HfNbTaTiZr samples at selected temperatures within the 500°C to 1200°C range. Concurrently, use high-resolution electron microscopy (or in situ neutron diffraction if possible) to characterize dislocation types (screw vs. edge) and assess short-range order changes. Parallel atomistic/mesoscale simulations should track dislocation core evolution and chemical ordering as a function of temperature under similar loading conditions.
measurements: Elastic moduli (Young’s, shear, and bulk) via in situ techniques
Dislocation density and character (quantification of screw versus edge components) using TEM or similar
Short-range order parameters from diffraction studies or atomistic simulation outputs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical measurements do not show a deviation from room temperature behavior (i.e., no significant softening or anomalous thermal expansion) or if microscopic analysis and simulations do not detect any increase in edge dislocation activity or changes in short-range order across the temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5.
